title: Conservatives and Liberals
q: A statesman argues that hereditary monarchy, an established church, and traditional social ranks are necessary barriers against revolutionary chaos. Which ideology best matches his position?
opts: Conservatism
Liberalism
Nationalism
Socialism
explanation: Conservatives defended inherited institutions, social hierarchy, monarchy, and organized religion because they associated rapid change with the violence of the French Revolution. Liberals favored constitutions and individual rights; nationalists emphasized shared identity and statehood; socialists focused on economic class and ownership.

title: Liberal Goals
q: Which reform would a European liberal of the early 1800s be most likely to support?
opts: The restoration of unlimited royal authority to preserve domestic order
The reservation of permanent control over legislatures for aristocrats
The creation of a written constitution to protect individual liberties
The suppression of all independent newspapers criticizing the monarchy
explanation: Nineteenth-century liberals generally supported constitutional government, equality before the law, private property, religious toleration, and freedom of speech and press. Unlimited monarchy, aristocratic privilege, and censorship were conservative policies liberals opposed.

title: Conservative and Liberal Beliefs
q: Which positions were commonly associated with nineteenth-century liberalism? Select all that apply.
correct: Establishment of government based on a written constitution
Protection of civil liberties such as free speech and press
Guarantee of legal equality for all citizens before the law
opts: Establishment of government based on a written constitution
Protection of civil liberties such as free speech and press
Guarantee of legal equality for all citizens before the law
Restoration of traditional feudal privileges for landowners
Permanent censorship of political criticism against the state
explanation: Liberals sought constitutional limits, civil liberties, and legal equality. Feudal privilege and permanent censorship protected the old order and therefore aligned more closely with conservatism.

title: Nationalism
q: People who share a language, culture, history, and traditions demand that scattered territories be united under one government. Their demand is primarily an expression of:
opts: Absolutism
Nationalism
Imperialism
Liberalism
explanation: Nationalism holds that people joined by a common identity should form or control their own political state. Absolutism concerns royal power, mercantilism concerns state-regulated trade, and laissez-faire concerns limited economic regulation.

title: Nationalism as a Force
q: Why could nationalism both unify and divide nineteenth-century Europe?
opts: It consistently strengthened multinational empires by creating a single, shared identity for all citizens.
It encouraged states to cooperate in global alliances while preventing any localized domestic conflicts.
It focused exclusively on expanding royal authority and restoring traditional, feudal economic structures.
It united culturally related groups in divided lands while driving ethnic minorities in empires to rebel.
explanation: Nationalism helped unite Germany and Italy, but it also weakened the Austrian and Ottoman empires by inspiring subject peoples to demand autonomy or statehood. Its effect depended on whether a national group was politically divided or trapped inside a multinational empire.

title: Congress of Vienna
q: What was the central goal of the Congress of Vienna after Napoleon's defeat?
opts: To restore stability through legitimacy and a balance of power
To establish democratic republics across the European continent
To support immediate national unification for Germany and Italy
To enforce the immediate abolition of all European monarchies
explanation: The Congress sought stability by restoring legitimate dynasties, containing France, and balancing the great powers so no state could dominate Europe. It was conservative and did not aim to spread republics or national unification.

title: Metternich and the Vienna Settlement
q: Klemens von Metternich would most likely view liberal and nationalist movements as dangerous because they:
opts: Directly enhanced the political dominance of Austria over Europe
Actively protected the divine right of every traditional dynasty
Threatened monarchic rule and the unity of multinational empires
Prevented ordinary citizens from demanding written constitutions
explanation: As an Austrian conservative, Metternich feared that constitutional demands would weaken rulers and nationalism would tear apart the Habsburg Empire's many ethnic groups. The movements undermined rather than protected the old order.

title: Vienna Settlement Methods
q: Which actions reflected the Congress of Vienna's conservative settlement? Select all that apply.
correct: Restoring traditional, displaced royal dynasties
Strengthening neighboring states around France
Creating a stable balance among the great powers
opts: Restoring traditional, displaced royal dynasties
Strengthening neighboring states around France
Creating a stable balance among the great powers
Granting universal voting rights to all citizens
Recognizing ethnic groups as independent states
explanation: Restoration, containment, and balance of power were core Vienna principles. Universal suffrage and national self-determination would have challenged the monarchies and borders the delegates were trying to preserve.

title: Serbian and Greek Independence
q: The Serbian and Greek revolts were similar because both movements:
opts: Sought complete independence from the Austrian Empire
Challenged Ottoman rule by rallying national identity
Restored French imperial control throughout the region
Opposed the concept of shared ethnic and cultural ties
explanation: Both Serbs and Greeks used national identity to resist Ottoman authority. Serbia gained substantial autonomy after revolts beginning in 1804, and Greece won recognized independence in 1830.

title: Belgian Revolution
q: Which combination best explains Belgium's successful revolt against Dutch rule in 1830?
opts: Agreement on religious policies and equal parliamentary representation under the House of Orange.
The sudden collapse of the Dutch economy combined with widespread support from Austrian forces.
Religious differences, inadequate representation, and inspiration from the French July Revolution.
A Prussian military occupation that forced the Dutch to cede their southern provinces to France.
explanation: Catholic Belgians resented rule by the largely Protestant Dutch and felt politically and economically neglected. The French July Revolution showed that a government could be overthrown, encouraging Belgian action.

title: France after Napoleon
q: Why did Louis XVIII face opposition after being restored to the French throne?
opts: He immediately declared a republic and transferred all executive power to a radical assembly.
He refused to sign the Charter of Liberties or permit a representative national legislature.
He aligned exclusively with the middle class while completely ignoring the landed aristocracy.
His constitutional compromise satisfied neither hard-line royalists nor reform-minded liberals.
explanation: Louis XVIII accepted the Charter of French Liberties, attempting to combine monarchy with limited constitutionalism. Ultra-royalists thought he conceded too much, while liberals believed the settlement did not protect enough rights or participation.

title: July Revolution
q: What most directly caused Charles X to lose the French throne in the July Revolution of 1830?
opts: His attempt to restore stronger absolute rule, suspend the legislature, and restrict press freedom.
His public support for universal male suffrage and the direct election of local government officials.
His formal alliance with radical socialists to dismantle private property rights across the nation.
His controversial decision to close the Catholic Church and ban all public religious celebrations.
explanation: Charles X's reactionary policies and July Ordinances restricted the press and political participation, provoking revolt. He abdicated, and Louis-Philippe became the constitutional 'Citizen King.'

title: Causes of the 1848 French Revolution
q: Which conditions contributed to revolution in France in February 1848? Select all that apply.
correct: Widespread economic recession and factory closures
Severe food shortages and rapidly rising crop prices
Government corruption and the repression of protests
opts: Widespread economic recession and factory closures
Severe food shortages and rapidly rising crop prices
Government corruption and the repression of protests
A prolonged period of universal economic prosperity
The expansion of voting rights to all adult citizens
explanation: Recession, unemployment, food scarcity, corruption, and the government's violent response to protest destroyed support for Louis-Philippe. Prosperity and universal voting rights did not characterize his government.

title: Second Republic
q: What was France's Second Republic?
opts: The centralized absolute monarchy established by Charles X before the July Revolution of 1830.
The republican government created after Louis-Philippe abdicated during the 1848 revolution.
The authoritarian imperial regime declared by Emperor Napoleon III following his coup in 1852.
The new constitutional system established immediately following the end of the Napoleonic Wars.
explanation: The February Revolution of 1848 ended Louis-Philippe's monarchy and produced the Second Republic. It was later destroyed when Louis-Napoleon staged a coup and became Emperor Napoleon III.

title: June Days
q: The June Days uprising of 1848 revealed which major division inside the new French republic?
opts: A geopolitical conflict between the French republic and the British Empire
A religious conflict between the Catholic majority and Protestant minorities
A class conflict between urban workers and middle- and upper-class liberals
A political dispute over whether to restore feudal serfdom in rural areas
explanation: Workers rebelled after the government closed the National Workshops that had provided employment. The violent suppression, which killed about 1,500 citizens, exposed the republic's sharp class divisions.

title: Louis-Napoleon
q: How did Louis-Napoleon transform the Second Republic?
opts: He surrendered all executive authority to the National Assembly and retired from public life.
He restored the Orleans monarchy by returning the aging Louis-Philippe to the French throne.
He signed a treaty that voluntarily integrated the French state into the growing German Empire.
He used a coup to dissolve the republican government and declared himself Emperor Napoleon III.
explanation: Elected president in 1848, Louis-Napoleon later dissolved the National Assembly in a coup and established authoritarian rule, becoming Emperor Napoleon III. His rise ended the Second Republic.

title: Revolutions of 1848
q: Why did many European revolutions of 1848 fail despite early successes?
opts: Revolutionaries were divided, and conservative armies recovered and suppressed the rebellions.
European monarchs voluntarily abdicated their thrones and accepted national self-determination.
Working-class radicals and middle-class liberals agreed on all economic and political goals.
Foreign military powers consistently refused to intervene to support conservative governments.
explanation: Liberal, nationalist, and working-class revolutionaries often wanted different outcomes. Once frightened elites regrouped, loyal armies and foreign intervention restored conservative control in Austria, Italy, and much of Germany.

title: Frankfurt Assembly
q: Why did Frederick William IV's rejection of a crown offered by the Frankfurt Assembly damage the cause of German unity in 1848?
opts: It allowed the Austrian Empire to annex all of northern Germany and establish direct imperial control over Prussia.
It showed that liberal nationalists lacked the military power to enforce unification without monarchical support.
It led to the immediate creation of a unified German republic under the joint leadership of France and Russia.
It dissolved the Prussian state entirely and divided its lands among the surrounding minor German principalities.
explanation: The Frankfurt Assembly depended on voluntary cooperation from established rulers. Frederick William's refusal demonstrated that speeches and constitutions alone could not overcome monarchical and military power.

title: Atlantic Revolutions
q: Which two broad conditions encouraged independence movements in Latin America?
opts: The decline of Enlightenment philosophy and stronger Spanish imperial control
The expansion of British colonies and direct military support from North America
The spread of Enlightenment philosophy and political chaos in European empires
The Congress of Vienna's formal declaration supporting colonial independence
explanation: Ideas of natural rights and popular sovereignty crossed the Atlantic, while Napoleon's invasions disrupted Spain and Portugal. Colonial elites and other groups used the crisis to challenge imperial authority.

title: Haitian Revolution
q: Why was the Haitian Revolution historically unique?
opts: It was the only large-scale slave revolt to successfully create a new, independent nation.
It successfully preserved the institution of plantation slavery under a French royal governor.
It established a permanent European-style absolute monarchy that dominated the Caribbean.
It succeeded entirely through peaceful negotiations without any outbreak of military conflict.
explanation: Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue defeated major imperial armies and created independent Haiti in 1804. The revolution directly challenged slavery, colonialism, and racial hierarchy in a way unmatched by other Atlantic revolutions.

title: Toussaint L'Ouverture
q: What best explains Toussaint L'Ouverture's success as a revolutionary leader?
opts: He relied on permanent French military assistance and financial aid from the British government.
He built a disciplined army and skillfully shifted alliances among competing European empires.
He refused to govern Saint-Domingue, leaving administrative duties to Spanish colonial officials.
He restored the system of plantation slavery to win the support of wealthy European landowners.
explanation: Toussaint combined military organization, political leadership, and flexible diplomacy while French, Spanish, and British forces competed in the Caribbean. Although Napoleon captured him, the movement he helped build survived and won independence.

title: Haitian Revolution Outcomes
q: Which were consequences or historical meanings of the Haitian Revolution? Select all that apply.
correct: Haiti established political independence from France
The revolution directly challenged Atlantic slavery
Slaveholding societies feared similar slave uprisings
opts: Haiti established political independence from France
The revolution directly challenged Atlantic slavery
Slaveholding societies feared similar slave uprisings
France permanently restored slavery in the territory
Spain peacefully annexed the colony of Saint-Domingue
explanation: Haitian independence destroyed slavery in the colony and frightened slaveholding elites throughout the Atlantic world. France did not retain Haiti, and Spain did not inherit it.

title: Mexican Independence
q: Which sequence best describes Mexico's path to independence?
opts: Spanish authorities voluntarily granted autonomy in 1808, avoiding any armed rebellion or civil war.
The Creole elite led a peaceful transition of power, establishing a stable republic without a revolt.
Liberal reformers overthrew the viceroy in 1810, leading to immediate annexation by the United States.
Hidalgo began a mass revolt in 1810, and Iturbide later secured independence as a conservative leader.
explanation: Father Miguel Hidalgo launched the 1810 rebellion but was captured and executed. After years of conflict, conservative Creole officer Agustin de Iturbide joined the independence cause and secured separation from Spain in 1821.

title: Hidalgo's Movement
q: Why did many wealthy Creoles initially fear Miguel Hidalgo's independence movement?
opts: It promised to restore heavy Spanish taxes and re-establish the absolute authority of the crown.
It was led exclusively by high-ranking Spanish officials who wanted to restrict colonial trade.
Its mass support among Indigenous people and mestizos threatened their own economic and social power.
It demanded that Mexico abolish all private landownership and merge with neighboring territories.
explanation: Hidalgo mobilized poor and racially marginalized groups, making elites fear social revolution as well as political separation. This helps explain why Mexican independence eventually succeeded through an alliance that protected elite interests.

title: Simon Bolivar
q: Which description best identifies Simon Bolivar?
opts: A prominent Creole leader who helped liberate northern South America from Spanish rule.
A Spanish general who successfully restored imperial control over the territory of Haiti.
An Austrian diplomat who designed the European balance of power at the Congress of Vienna.
A revolutionary Mexican priest who launched the independence war with the Grito de Dolores.
explanation: Bolivar, known as El Libertador, led campaigns that helped free Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. Hidalgo issued the Grito de Dolores; Metternich was the Austrian diplomat.

title: Gran Colombia
q: Why did Bolivar's dream of a durable, united Gran Colombia fail?
opts: Spain launched a major military campaign that quickly reconquered the South American colonies.
Regional rivalries, geographic barriers, and competing local elites caused it to split apart.
Bolivar decided to dissolve the state and support the restoration of Spanish monarchical rule.
The United States military invaded the region and annexed all the newly independent territories.
explanation: Mountains and distance complicated government, while regional caudillos and local elites resisted centralized authority. Gran Colombia broke into separate states even though Spain did not reconquer them.

title: Latin American Independence
q: Which factors limited unity and stability after Latin American independence? Select all that apply.
correct: Intense regional rivalries among local caudillos
Difficult geography and weak transport networks
Persistent social and ethnic inequality systems
opts: Intense regional rivalries among local caudillos
Difficult geography and weak transport networks
Persistent social and ethnic inequality systems
Complete consensus over centralized governments
The total collapse of elite-owned landholdings
explanation: Caudillo rivalry, geographic barriers, and inherited inequality made unified government difficult. Independence did not erase elite landownership or create consensus about political structure.

title: German Confederation
q: What was the German Confederation created after the Napoleonic Wars?
opts: A democratic nation-state led by the Prussian monarchy
An overseas colony controlled by French administrators
A weak association of German states dominated by Austria
A military union between Germany and the Italian states
explanation: The Congress of Vienna replaced Napoleon's arrangements with a loose confederation of 39 states. Metternich favored its weakness because Austrian influence and conservative rulers would be safer than in a strong united Germany.

title: Bismarck's Background
q: Bismarck's identity as a Prussian Junker meant that he came from:
opts: The urban socialist industrial class
The Catholic clerical establishment
A radical French republican family
The conservative landowning nobility
explanation: Junkers were Prussian landed nobles who traditionally supported the monarchy and army. Bismarck's background helps explain his conservatism and loyalty to Prussian power.

title: Realpolitik
q: What did Bismarck's mastery of Realpolitik involve?
opts: Using practical power calculations rather than fixed ideals
Submitting all major policies to popular national referendums
Rejecting both diplomacy and warfare under all circumstances
Making religious doctrine the sole basis of his foreign policy
explanation: Realpolitik emphasized achievable results, military strength, strategic alliances, and calculated compromise. Bismarck could cooperate with one state and later oppose it if Prussian interests changed.

title: Blood and Iron
q: Bismarck's 'blood and iron' speech most clearly expressed his belief that German unification would be achieved through:
opts: Literary nationalism and cultural education
Military strength and decisive state actions
Austrian diplomatic and political leadership
A radical socialist working-class revolution
explanation: Bismarck argued that the major questions of the age would not be settled by speeches and parliamentary votes alone. He strengthened the Prussian army and used limited wars to reshape Germany.

title: Wars of German Unification
q: Which conflicts did Bismarck use to expand Prussian power and unify Germany? Select all that apply.
correct: The War against Denmark
The Austro-Prussian War
The Franco-Prussian War
opts: The War against Denmark
The Austro-Prussian War
The Franco-Prussian War
The Russian Crimean War
The Greek Revolution War
explanation: The Danish, Austro-Prussian, and Franco-Prussian wars isolated opponents and rallied German states behind Prussia. The Crimean and Greek wars were not stages of Bismarck's unification strategy.

title: Austro-Prussian War
q: What was the most important political result of Prussia's rapid victory over Austria in 1866?
opts: Austria annexed all Prussian territory and established direct control over northern German states.
France assumed absolute political control over all German principalities to block Prussian expansion.
Austria was excluded from German affairs, allowing Prussia to lead the North German Confederation.
The German Confederation was restructured to grant Metternich permanent executive power in Berlin.
explanation: The Seven Weeks' War ended Austrian leadership in Germany and allowed Prussia to organize the North German Confederation. This established the foundation for a Prussian-led nation-state.

title: Ems Dispatch
q: Why did Bismarck edit and publish the Ems Dispatch in 1870?
opts: To prevent any future military conflict with France by offering permanent territorial concessions.
To formally invite the Austrian Empire back into a leadership role within the German Confederation.
To negotiate a peaceful resolution and announce a diplomatic compromise over the Spanish throne.
To provoke French outrage and unite the southern German states against a common external threat.
explanation: Bismarck shortened the diplomatic report so both France and Prussia appeared insulted. France declared war, and the southern German states joined Prussia, completing national unification after victory.

title: German Constitution
q: How did the constitution of the new German Empire combine popular participation with elite control?
opts: The Reichstag was elected by universal male suffrage, but the appointed chancellor and Bundesrat held real power.
Both chambers of parliament were directly elected by all adult men and women under a system of equal votes.
The emperor served only as a powerless figurehead while all executive authority was held by elected officials.
The Reichstag was given the absolute constitutional power to remove the ruling emperor by a simple majority vote.
explanation: Adult men elected the Reichstag, but the Bundesrat represented state rulers and could block it. The emperor appointed the chancellor, so executive and aristocratic power remained strong despite elections.

title: German Industrial Growth
q: Which factors helped unified Germany become an industrial giant? Select all that apply.
correct: Abundant domestic reserves of both coal and iron
A single currency and unified national banking
Industrial investment and a disciplined workforce
Rapid population growth expanding the labor pool
opts: Abundant domestic reserves of both coal and iron
A single currency and unified national banking
Industrial investment and a disciplined workforce
Rapid population growth expanding the labor pool
Strict national bans on foreign technology use
explanation: Natural resources, financial unity, investment, labor, and population growth encouraged rapid industrialization. A ban on factories and railroads would have prevented rather than accelerated growth.

title: Bismarck's Foreign Policy
q: After unification, Bismarck's primary foreign-policy strategy was to:
opts: Prepare an immediate military invasion of Great Britain to seize control of its global trade routes.
Keep France isolated while maintaining workable ties with Austria and Russia to avoid a two-front war.
Expand German territories by launching rapid invasions of neighboring Denmark and the Swiss cantons.
Build a formal military alliance with France and Russia to dismantle the neighboring Austrian Empire.
explanation: Bismarck regarded satisfied, secure Germany as needing peace. He tried to prevent France from finding allies and managed relations among Austria and Russia to avoid a two-front war.

title: Kulturkampf
q: Bismarck's Kulturkampf was an effort to:
opts: Promote cultural unity by integrating the German and French states
Expand the political influence of the Catholic pope within Germany
Reduce the Catholic Church's influence and strengthen state loyalty
Suppress the growing socialist movement and outlaw all trade unions
explanation: Bismarck feared that Catholics might place loyalty to the pope above loyalty to the empire. His campaign restricted Church influence, although resistance eventually forced him to retreat from several measures.

title: William II and Bismarck
q: Why did Kaiser William II remove Bismarck from power?
opts: Bismarck advocated for surrendering Alsace-Lorraine and returning Germany to direct French control.
The elected Reichstag voted to legally abolish the office of the chancellor to increase democracy.
Bismarck refused to serve the new monarch and publicly declared his support for a British alliance.
The young emperor wanted to rule personally and disagreed with Bismarck's cautious foreign policy.
explanation: William II declared that there would be only one master in the Reich. Personal rivalry and policy disagreements led him to demand Bismarck's resignation in 1890.

title: William II's Germany
q: Which policy most clearly distinguished William II from Bismarck?
opts: A major naval buildup designed to rival Great Britain
The total avoidance of overseas colonial competition
The restoration of the pre-unification confederation
The elimination of all basic social welfare programs
explanation: William II pursued a more aggressive world policy and greatly expanded the navy, alarming Britain. He also adopted some welfare measures, so eliminating all social programs is incorrect.

title: Mazzini and Young Italy
q: What was Giuseppe Mazzini's contribution to Italian unification?
opts: He actively defended Austrian rule in northern Italy and opposed all local national rebellions.
He founded Young Italy and promoted a united nation based on shared language and cultural identity.
He served as Pope Pius IX and used the church's spiritual authority to oppose Italian nationalism.
He commanded the Prussian military forces that defeated the Austrian Empire during the war of 1866.
explanation: Mazzini supplied ideological inspiration through Young Italy, arguing that Italians shared a historical and cultural identity. His revolts often failed, but his nationalism shaped later unification.

title: Cavour's Strategy
q: Why did Cavour bring Sardinia-Piedmont into the Crimean War?
opts: To launch a military campaign designed to conquer the Russian Empire and establish permanent colonies.
To support Austrian control over northern Italy by forming a defensive alliance with Vienna's rulers.
To gain diplomatic influence with Britain and France for the purpose of challenging Austrian power.
To provide military assistance that would help Giuseppe Garibaldi overthrow the French royal dynasty.
explanation: Sardinia's military contribution was small, but participation earned Cavour a place at the peace talks. He used that visibility to win support, especially from Napoleon III, against Austria.

title: Cavour and Garibaldi
q: Which statement best contrasts Cavour and Garibaldi?
opts: Both leaders completely avoided warfare, relying instead on peaceful petitions sent to Austrian rulers.
Garibaldi acted as a cautious diplomat in the north, while Cavour commanded the Red Shirts in the south.
Both figures actively opposed Italian unification and wanted to keep the peninsula permanently divided.
Cavour used diplomacy and monarchy in the north, while Garibaldi relied on military force in the south.
explanation: Cavour directed Sardinia-Piedmont's statecraft and alliances. Garibaldi and his Red Shirts conquered Sicily and Naples, then transferred those lands to Victor Emmanuel II.

title: Italian Unification Leaders
q: Which leader-role pairings are accurate? Select all that apply.
correct: Mazzini - the founder of the Young Italy movement
Cavour - Sardinian prime minister and key diplomat
Garibaldi - the leader of the volunteer Red Shirts
Victor Emmanuel II - the monarch of unified Italy
opts: Mazzini - the founder of the Young Italy movement
Cavour - Sardinian prime minister and key diplomat
Garibaldi - the leader of the volunteer Red Shirts
Victor Emmanuel II - the monarch of unified Italy
Metternich - conservative leader of the Red Shirts
explanation: Mazzini inspired, Cavour maneuvered diplomatically, Garibaldi conquered in the south, and Victor Emmanuel II became king. Metternich was an Austrian conservative who opposed Italian nationalism.

title: Foreign Powers and Italy
q: How did foreign affairs assist Italian unification?
opts: French aid helped Sardinia defeat Austria, and subsequent wars allowed Italy to acquire Venetia and Rome.
Austrian rulers voluntarily ceded their northern territories and financed the Italian unification process.
Russian armies conquered the peninsula and directly transferred control of all Italian states to Sardinia.
British forces intervened directly in the south and officially installed Giuseppe Garibaldi as the emperor.
explanation: Cavour secured Napoleon III's assistance against Austria. Later, the Austro-Prussian and Franco-Prussian wars created opportunities for Italy to gain Venetia and Rome.

title: Problems of Unified Italy
q: Which problems confronted Italy after unification? Select all that apply.
correct: Deep-seated regional divisions and dialects
Ongoing political conflict with the papacy
Rising political turmoil and socialist growth
Uneven industrialization and mass emigration
opts: Deep-seated regional divisions and dialects
Ongoing political conflict with the papacy
Rising political turmoil and socialist growth
Uneven industrialization and mass emigration
Complete domination by Prussian military forces
explanation: Political borders did not instantly create a shared identity or equal economy. Regional division, Church hostility, social conflict, industrial disruption, and migration remained major challenges.

title: Making Italians
q: The statement 'We have made Italy; now we must make Italians' means that:
opts: The country still lacked recognized legal borders and international treaty rights.
Political unification had occurred, but a common national identity still had to be forged.
Austrian forces still ruled directly over every independent state in the peninsula.
All citizens already shared a single, uniform language and national cultural heritage.
explanation: Many residents identified more strongly with region, town, or dialect than with the new nation. The state therefore had to build common institutions and loyalty after formal unification.

title: Britain's Two Nations
q: In Benjamin Disraeli's description of Britain as 'two nations,' the two groups were:
opts: The industrial manufacturers and agricultural workers
The Anglican church leaders and nonconformist citizens
The wealthy upper classes and the impoverished workers
The English population and the French speaking minority
explanation: Disraeli emphasized the social separation between wealthy and impoverished Britons created or intensified by industrial society. The phrase highlighted class inequality, not international rivalry.

title: Parliamentary Representation
q: Why were rotten boroughs criticized before the Reform Act of 1832?
opts: They gave rapidly growing industrial cities an unfair number of representatives.
They allowed parliamentary members to be elected through universal male suffrage.
They were heavily influenced and financially controlled by radical labor unions.
They retained their seats in Parliament despite having very few actual voters.
explanation: Tiny or nearly abandoned districts could send members to Parliament, while rapidly growing industrial cities were underrepresented. This made representation unequal and vulnerable to aristocratic control.

title: Reform Act of 1832
q: What did the Reform Act of 1832 accomplish?
opts: It expanded the electorate and redistributed parliamentary seats to growing industrial towns.
It granted adult women full voting rights and allowed them to hold parliamentary office.
It established universal male suffrage and removed all property qualifications for voting.
It introduced the secret ballot for all elections to prevent aristocratic corruption.
explanation: The act eliminated many rotten borough seats, gave more representation to industrial areas, and expanded voting among property-owning men. It was important but did not create universal suffrage or enfranchise women.

title: Chartist Demands
q: Which reforms were associated with the Chartist movement? Select all that apply.
correct: Universal suffrage for all adult men
Introduction of the secret ballot
Equal electoral districts across Britain
opts: Universal suffrage for all adult men
Introduction of the secret ballot
Equal electoral districts across Britain
Hereditary seats for industrial capitalists
Absolute veto power for the reigning monarch
explanation: Chartists demanded a more democratic Parliament, especially for working men. Secret voting and fairer districts would reduce elite control; abolishing elections or strengthening hereditary rule would do the opposite.

title: Victorian Political Reform
q: Which statement best evaluates Victorian parliamentary reform?
opts: Britain instantly transformed into a complete democracy with the passage of the 1832 reform.
Voting rights and House of Commons power expanded gradually, but women remained disenfranchised.
The House of Lords obtained permanent veto power over all financial and tax legislation in 1911.
The Conservative and Liberal parties merged into a single governing body to prevent elections.
explanation: A series of reforms broadened male suffrage, adopted the secret ballot, and reduced the Lords' power. The process was gradual and incomplete; British women did not gain parliamentary voting rights until 1918.

title: Victorian Ideals
q: Which values were most closely associated with Victorian ideals?
opts: Individual liberty, free expression, and secularism
Military dominance, state control, and absolute obedience
Hard work, personal thrift, duty, honesty, and loyalty
Collectivism, economic equality, and community ownership
explanation: Victorian culture publicly celebrated discipline, responsibility, thrift, honesty, and loyalty. These ideals coexisted with severe class inequality and imperial expansion.

title: Corn Laws
q: Why did industrial and urban interests favor repeal of the Corn Laws?
opts: They believed that higher tariffs on foreign imports would protect domestic factories.
They wanted to safeguard the high profits of aristocratic agricultural landowners.
They opposed international commerce and sought complete economic self-sufficiency.
They argued that cheaper imported grain would lower food costs and promote free trade.
explanation: The Corn Laws protected British grain producers with tariffs, keeping food prices high. Manufacturers and urban consumers favored repeal because cheaper food benefited workers and supported free trade.

title: British Social Reforms
q: Which changes represented social or political reform in nineteenth-century Britain? Select all that apply.
correct: The abolition of the slave trade in 1807
The total abolition of slavery in 1833
The legal expansion of active labor unions
The reduction in the number of capital crimes
opts: The abolition of the slave trade in 1807
The total abolition of slavery in 1833
The legal expansion of active labor unions
The reduction in the number of capital crimes
The permanent restriction of all foreign trade
explanation: Britain ended the slave trade, abolished slavery in most of its empire, reduced harsh criminal penalties, and increasingly recognized unions. Restoring slavery was not a reform.

title: Labour Party
q: The emergence of the Labour Party in 1900 most directly reflected:
opts: The growing political organization of workers seeking social reform and welfare legislation.
The rapid decline of industrial factories and the disappearance of the urban working class.
A coordinated campaign by the aristocracy to strengthen rotten boroughs in rural districts.
A concerted effort by wealthy landowners to restrict all international trade and free markets.
explanation: Trade unionists and social reformers wanted direct representation for working-class interests and welfare legislation. Industrial labor had expanded, not disappeared.

title: Irish Grievances
q: Which issues fueled Irish nationalism under British rule? Select all that apply.
correct: High rents paid to absentee British landlords
Required tithes to support the Anglican Church
Devastating famine during the Great Hunger
Denials of Catholic rights and local Home Rule
opts: High rents paid to absentee British landlords
Required tithes to support the Anglican Church
Devastating famine during the Great Hunger
Denials of Catholic rights and local Home Rule
Overwhelming competition from French merchants
explanation: Landlordism, religious discrimination, famine, and limited self-government generated resentment. Daniel O'Connell pursued Catholic emancipation, while later moderates sought Home Rule and radicals pursued independence.

title: Napoleon III's Domestic Rule
q: How did Napoleon III's domestic government change during his reign?
opts: It started as a constitutional democracy but became increasingly absolutist and repressive.
It began as an authoritarian dictatorship but gradually allowed more political liberalization.
It focused exclusively on agricultural development while banning all railway construction.
It surrendered all executive authority to the revolutionary leaders of the Paris Commune.
explanation: Napoleon III initially ruled as an authoritarian emperor, restricting opposition. In the 1860s he liberalized parts of the regime, though France did not become a fully parliamentary democracy.

title: Suez Canal
q: What was the purpose of the Suez Canal, and how was France connected to it?
opts: It connected the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and was constructed by German military engineers.
It linked the Rhine and Danube rivers and was funded exclusively by British commercial banks.
It connected the Mediterranean and Red seas and was built by a French-led development company.
It carried railway transport across the Swiss Alps and was designed by Italian state engineers.
explanation: The canal created a much shorter route between Europe and the Indian Ocean. Ferdinand de Lesseps and a French-led company developed it, though Britain later acquired major shares and strategic influence.

title: Napoleon III's Foreign Policy
q: Which statements accurately describe Napoleon III's foreign-policy record? Select all that apply.
correct: He won prestige in the Crimean War but gained little for its cost
He supported Italian nationalists in their conflict with Austria
His attempt to establish a satellite monarchy in Mexico failed
He was defeated and captured during the Franco-Prussian War
opts: He won prestige in the Crimean War but gained little for its cost
He supported Italian nationalists in their conflict with Austria
His attempt to establish a satellite monarchy in Mexico failed
He was defeated and captured during the Franco-Prussian War
He successfully established a permanent French colony in Egypt
explanation: Napoleon III had mixed early successes, but the Mexican adventure collapsed and the Franco-Prussian War destroyed his empire. France never annexed Prussia.

title: Fall of Napoleon III
q: What event directly ended Napoleon III's rule?
opts: The outbreak of democratic revolutions across Europe in 1848
The economic depression caused by the building of the Suez Canal
The political crisis surrounding the start of the Dreyfus Affair
His military capture following the defeat at Sedan in 1870
explanation: Prussian forces defeated and captured Napoleon III at Sedan during the Franco-Prussian War. The empire collapsed, and France proclaimed the Third Republic.

title: Paris Commune
q: What was the Paris Commune of 1871?
opts: A radical municipal government in Paris that resisted the conservative national assembly.
A regional Prussian assembly established to govern French territory captured in the war.
A royalist coalition that successfully restored the empire under Napoleon III's heirs.
A peaceful labor union officially recognized and sponsored by the German chancellor.
explanation: Radicals and socialists in Paris rejected the national government's surrender and authority. Civil war followed, and government troops crushed the Commune during a bloody campaign.

title: Suppression of the Commune
q: What did the suppression of the Paris Commune demonstrate?
opts: France had successfully resolved its deep class divisions through peaceful political compromise.
The Third Republic was willing to use extreme violence to suppress working-class radicalism.
Prussia intended to establish a permanent military occupation and govern the city of Paris.
Socialist and anarchist leaders had obtained full command of the official French army.
explanation: Thousands were killed, arrested, or deported when the army retook Paris. The episode revealed the deep divide between radical workers and the more conservative national government.

title: Third Republic Government
q: Why did coalition governments become common in France's Third Republic?
opts: Only a single political party was legally permitted to run candidates for parliament.
The executive president ruled as an absolute monarch and dissolved all opposition parties.
Many parties shared the legislature, requiring alliances to form a majority and govern.
The national army directly appointed all members of the assembly to ensure stability.
explanation: The Third Republic had a two-house legislature and numerous political parties. Because no single party consistently held a majority, cabinets depended on coalitions led by a premier.

title: Dreyfus Affair
q: Why did the Dreyfus Affair divide French society so deeply?
opts: Alfred Dreyfus openly confessed to espionage, causing a collapse of public trust in the French republic.
The military evidence against the accused officer was completely uncontested by all legal experts.
The entire legal controversy centered on a minor tax dispute between the army and wealthy landowners.
A Jewish officer was falsely convicted of treason, exposing deep antisemitism and dividing the nation.
explanation: Forged and concealed evidence kept Alfred Dreyfus imprisoned while nationalists and antisemites defended the military. Supporters demanded justice and civilian accountability, creating a major political and cultural split.

title: Dreyfus and Zionism
q: How did the Dreyfus Affair influence Theodor Herzl?
opts: It convinced him that Jewish people required a secure national homeland.
It led him to reject all nationalist movements and support globalism.
It inspired him to enlist as a high-ranking officer in the French army.
It persuaded him that antisemitic prejudice had finally been eliminated.
explanation: Herzl saw that even an assimilated Jewish officer in republican France could become a target of antisemitism. He became a leading advocate of political Zionism and a Jewish homeland.

title: Habsburg Nationalities
q: Why was nationalism especially dangerous to the Habsburg Empire?
opts: The vast majority of the imperial population already shared a single, common language.
The empire ruled many nationalities, while German-speaking Austrians were a small minority.
The ruling dynasty had already voluntarily granted full independence to all ethnic groups.
Nationalist demands served to reinforce absolute imperial unity under Metternich's central rule.
explanation: The Habsburg lands included Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks, Poles, Italians, Croats, Serbs, Romanians, and others. National demands therefore threatened to fragment the dynasty's multinational state.

title: Francis Joseph
q: How did Francis Joseph initially respond to the revolutions and nationalist pressures facing Austria?
opts: He voluntarily dissolved the Habsburg dynasty and permitted the immediate establishment of democratic republics.
He recognized all minority claims and granted complete political independence to every ethnic group in the realm.
He consolidated monarchical power while offering limited constitutional reforms that kept control in Austrian hands.
He appointed the Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Garibaldi to oversee the administrative government of the capital.
explanation: Francis Joseph became emperor during the crisis of 1848 and restored central authority. Constitutional concessions existed, but power remained concentrated among the monarchy and German-speaking Austrian elites.

title: Dual Monarchy
q: What created the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary in 1867?
opts: A decisive military victory by Austrian forces over the expanding kingdom of Prussia.
The successful siege and permanent conquest of Vienna by the Ottoman imperial army.
The complete political unification of Austria and the newly formed German Empire.
A political compromise after defeat by Prussia that granted Hungary its own parliament.
explanation: Austria's 1866 defeat weakened the monarchy and strengthened Hungarian demands. The Ausgleich created separate Austrian and Hungarian governments under Francis Joseph as emperor and king.

title: Limits of the Dual Monarchy
q: Why did the Dual Monarchy fail to solve Austria-Hungary's nationality problem?
opts: It favored German and Magyar elites while other national groups remained politically dominated.
It granted every ethnic minority their own independent parliament and self-governing assembly.
It completely abolished Hungarian political influence and concentrated all power in Vienna.
It led to a direct annexation of all Austrian territories by the neighboring Ottoman Empire.
explanation: The compromise satisfied many Hungarian demands but did not do the same for Czechs, Slovaks, Croats, Serbs, Romanians, and others. These groups continued to seek autonomy or independence.

title: Ottoman Decline
q: Which factors contributed to the Ottoman Empire's decline in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries? Select all that apply.
correct: Nationalist revolts among various subject peoples
Intense European competition for Ottoman territories
Military and economic weakness relative to industrial powers
opts: Nationalist revolts among various subject peoples
Intense European competition for Ottoman territories
Military and economic weakness relative to industrial powers
An absolute lack of external diplomatic intervention
Complete and permanent subjection of Balkan states
explanation: Nationalism weakened Ottoman control, while Russia, Austria, Britain, and others competed over Ottoman lands and influence. Industrial and military disadvantages made resistance difficult.

title: Sick Man of Europe
q: Calling the Ottoman Empire the 'sick man of Europe' implied that:
opts: It was rapidly developing into Europe's strongest and most advanced industrial state.
It was steadily weakening, and rival powers expected to profit from its collapse.
It had successfully unified all diverse Balkan populations under a single identity.
It had successfully launched a military campaign and conquered the Russian Empire.
explanation: The phrase described the empire's loss of territory and declining ability to resist foreign pressure. European powers disagreed over how to divide influence and prevent rivals from gaining too much.

title: Balkan Wars
q: Why did the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913 make the region a 'powder keg'?
opts: They permanently ended all nationalist sentiments and ethnic conflicts across southeastern Europe.
They created a stable and highly trusted military alliance that united all regional governments.
They intensified territorial rivalries and nationalism while rival great powers intervened for influence.
They restored complete and undisputed political control of all Balkan territories to the Ottoman Empire.
explanation: Balkan states fought the Ottomans and then one another over territory. National ambitions, unreliable alliances, and intervention by Austria-Hungary and Russia made a wider war increasingly likely.

title: Russia before Reform
q: Which feature made Russian modernization difficult in the mid-1800s?
opts: The rapid growth of a powerful, independent urban middle class.
The presence of universal education and broad political liberties.
The complete absence of wealthy, landowning noble aristocrats.
The persistence of serfdom, weak middle classes, and autocracy.
explanation: Russia remained dominated by nobles and an absolute monarchy, while millions of poor serfs had little mobility or purchasing power. These conditions slowed economic and political modernization.

title: Crimean War and Reform
q: Why did defeat in the Crimean War encourage Alexander II to reform Russia?
opts: It exposed Russia's severe military, transportation, and administrative weaknesses.
It demonstrated that the system of serfdom made Russian industry superior to Britain.
It successfully granted the Russian Empire direct control over all Ottoman territories.
It resulted in the immediate abdication of the tsar and the collapse of the monarchy.
explanation: Defeat by more industrialized powers showed that Russia's social and economic structure weakened its military. Alexander II concluded that reforms were necessary to preserve Russia as a great power.

title: Emancipation of the Serfs
q: What was Alexander II's most famous reform?
opts: Establishing the socialist Soviet Union in Eastern Europe
Emancipating millions of Russian serfs from land bondage
Completely abolishing the traditional Russian Orthodox Church
Granting full political independence to all subject nations
explanation: Alexander II freed the serfs in 1861. The reform was historic, but many peasants received inadequate land and heavy redemption payments, limiting its economic benefits.

title: Zemstvos
q: What were zemstvos?
opts: Elite secret police units designed to monitor political dissidents.
Private industrial factories owned and operated directly by the tsar.
Locally elected assemblies responsible for limited self-government.
National legislative bodies holding the power to remove the monarch.
explanation: Zemstvos handled local services such as roads, schools, and health. They introduced limited participation but did not replace autocracy or control national policy.

title: Alexander III's Reaction
q: How did Alexander III respond after Alexander II was assassinated?
opts: He embraced revolutionary socialist ideals and shared power with the working classes.
He immediately granted a fully democratic constitution and established free elections.
He ended all forms of discrimination against religious and ethnic minority groups.
He tightened autocratic rule, increased censorship, and repressed minority populations.
explanation: Alexander III reversed much of the reform spirit, strengthened censorship and police power, promoted Russian culture over minorities, and tolerated or encouraged violent antisemitic pogroms.

title: Russian Industrialization
q: Which tensions accompanied Russian industrialization under Alexander III and Nicholas II? Select all that apply.
correct: Severe and harsh urban working conditions
A growing and revolutionary labor movement
Widespread and continued peasant poverty
Strong autocratic resistance to political reform
opts: Severe and harsh urban working conditions
A growing and revolutionary labor movement
Widespread and continued peasant poverty
Strong autocratic resistance to political reform
Rapid and equal distribution of national wealth
explanation: Industrial growth expanded railways and factories but concentrated workers in difficult conditions. Peasant poverty and autocracy continued, creating rather than resolving revolutionary pressures.

title: Russo-Japanese War
q: Why did the Russo-Japanese War intensify Russia's domestic crisis?
opts: Unexpected defeats discredited the tsar and worsened economic conditions at home.
An easy and swift Russian victory made the tsar too popular to be challenged.
The Japanese military occupied Moscow and officially restored Russian serfdom.
The military conflict immediately forced the tsar to yield all power to the Duma.
explanation: Defeat by Japan shocked Russians who expected victory and exposed government incompetence. Wartime shortages and frustration contributed directly to the Revolution of 1905.

title: Bloody Sunday
q: Why was Bloody Sunday a turning point in 1905?
opts: A crowd of peaceful workers entered the palace and crowned Nicholas II.
Imperial troops fired on peaceful petitioners, destroying faith in the tsar.
The newly formed Duma ordered the military to launch an invasion of Japan.
The Russian Orthodox Church officially declared war on the absolute monarchy.
explanation: Workers marched peacefully to present grievances, but imperial troops killed and wounded protesters. The massacre triggered strikes, mutinies, and wider opposition to Nicholas II.

title: October Manifesto
q: What did Nicholas II promise in the October Manifesto?
opts: The permanent restoration of agrarian serfdom
The immediate abdication of the royal family
The grant of civil liberties and an elected Duma
A military union with the Austro-Hungarian Empire
explanation: Facing the Revolution of 1905, Nicholas promised basic freedoms and a national legislature. The concession divided the opposition and helped the regime survive temporarily.

title: Limits of the Duma
q: Why did the Duma fail to make Russia a stable constitutional monarchy?
opts: The assembly maintained absolute legislative control over the military budget.
The Duma voted to completely abolish the tsar's office and the monarchy.
The newly elected members flatly refused to assemble or pass any laws.
Nicholas II repeatedly dissolved critical Dumas and preserved absolute power.
explanation: The tsar accepted a legislature under pressure but did not accept genuine parliamentary control. He dismissed assemblies that challenged him and manipulated election laws.

title: Stolypin
q: What best characterizes Prime Minister Peter Stolypin's approach?
opts: Combining limited agrarian reforms with harsh repression of political dissidents.
Halting all imperial police actions and distributing land equally to peasants.
Drafting a constitutional plan to replace the tsar with an elected president.
Banning all private landownership and centralizing agricultural production.
explanation: Stolypin tried to create prosperous, conservative peasant landowners while using executions, arrests, and censorship against opponents. Reform and repression operated together.

title: Russia on the Eve of World War I
q: Which unresolved problems left Russia unstable by 1914? Select all that apply.
correct: Widespread peasant land hunger and poverty
Dangerous and poor urban working conditions
Extremely limited political power for the Duma
Systemic ethnic and religious group repression
Widespread loss of public trust in the tsar
opts: Widespread peasant land hunger and poverty
Dangerous and poor urban working conditions
Extremely limited political power for the Duma
Systemic ethnic and religious group repression
Widespread loss of public trust in the tsar
Total occupation of the capital by foreign forces
explanation: Russia had modernized unevenly without resolving land, labor, nationality, or constitutional questions. Nicholas II's defense of autocracy meant these pressures remained active when war began.

title: Comparing Unification
q: What was one major similarity between German and Italian unification?
opts: Both processes occurred entirely through peaceful agreements without any military conflict.
Both combined popular nationalist sentiment with leadership by a strong monarchical state.
Both movements resulted in the immediate establishment of constitutional, democratic republics.
Both unification campaigns were actively led and organized by Klemens von Metternich.
explanation: Prussia led German unification, while Sardinia-Piedmont led Italian unification. In both cases, nationalism mattered, but established monarchies, armies, and diplomatic leaders converted sentiment into state power.

title: Comparing Bismarck and Cavour
q: How were Bismarck and Cavour most alike?
opts: Both leaders were radical republicans who aimed to overthrow all royal dynasties.
Both statesmen consistently rejected any diplomatic alliances with foreign empires.
Both used pragmatic diplomacy and strategic wars to expand the power of their home states.
Both politicians actively worked to keep their regions under absolute Austrian control.
explanation: Neither leader was primarily an idealistic democrat. Bismarck served Prussia and Cavour served Sardinia-Piedmont, using alliances, calculation, and war to expand their states.

title: Revolution and Reform
q: Which broad pattern best describes political change in nineteenth-century Europe?
opts: Every popular uprising succeeded in establishing stable democratic governments immediately.
Conservative rulers successfully prevented any social or political reforms from occurring.
Nationalist movements and political revolutions exclusively affected the nation of France.
Even failed revolutions pressured conservative governments to adopt gradual reforms.
explanation: Many uprisings were crushed, but their demands did not disappear. Britain reformed gradually, France repeatedly changed regimes, Germany and Italy unified, and multinational empires faced growing national challenges.

title: Nationalism and Empire
q: Which examples show nationalism weakening multinational empires? Select all that apply.
correct: Greek resistance against Ottoman rule
Hungarian demands within the Habsburg Empire
Balkan movements against Ottoman control
Slavic autonomy demands in Austria-Hungary
opts: Greek resistance against Ottoman rule
Hungarian demands within the Habsburg Empire
Balkan movements against Ottoman control
Slavic autonomy demands in Austria-Hungary
British parliamentary repeal of the Corn Laws
explanation: Each correct example involved a national group challenging rule by a larger multinational empire. Repeal of the Corn Laws was an economic and parliamentary reform, not a nationalist revolt.

title: Nationalism and State Power
q: Which conclusion is best supported by the unifications of Germany and Italy?
opts: National ideals were most successful when joined to the military and diplomatic power of established states.
Poetic writers and student activists alone possessed the power to permanently defeat established empires.
Popular democratic elections served as the sole driving force behind the entire unification process.
Frequent foreign wars consistently prevented any progress toward establishing unified national states.
explanation: Mazzini and liberal nationalists inspired movements, but Cavour, Garibaldi, Bismarck, monarchs, armies, and international conflicts produced durable states. Ideas mattered most when connected to organized power.
